questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 35 weeks 4 days' gestation comes to the maternity assessment unit because her baby has moved much less than usual since the previous evening. Two years ago she had a stillbirth at 38 weeks, and that infant was small for gestational age. In this pregnancy she has diet-controlled gestational diabetes. A scan at 32 weeks showed an estimated weight on the 40th centile. She takes low-dose aspirin. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min and temperature is 36.7 °C. Symphysis-fundal height is 35 cm. A urine dipstick shows no protein. A 40-minute cardiotocograph (CTG) shows a baseline rate of 135 bpm, baseline variability of 10 bpm, three accelerations of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds, and no decelerations. She feels several movements during the trace.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day sonographic biometry and liquor volume assessment
Discharge with routine antenatal review at 37 weeks
Continuation of the CTG for a further 40 minutes
questions.explanation: Every feature of this CTG is normal by RANZCOG criteria: the baseline is 110 to 160 bpm, variability is 6 to 25 bpm, there are accelerations and there are no decelerations. Her observations and urinalysis show no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection. A normal CTG means the fetus is not hypoxic right now. It does not rule out underlying placental insufficiency or growth restriction, so it does not exclude a later poor outcome. The Stillbirth CRE guideline on decreased fetal movements says that when a woman has risk factors for growth restriction or stillbirth, she should have an ultrasound for fetal biometry and amniotic fluid volume, ideally within 24 hours, along with obstetric review. This woman has a previous small-for-gestational-age stillbirth and gestational diabetes. The scan should be arranged today. She should then be told to come back straight away, at any hour, if movements decrease again.
why: Sending her home with routine follow-up treats the normal CTG as if it rules out compromise, which is unsafe in a woman with risk factors for stillbirth.
A single episode of reduced movements with a normal CTG and a normal assessment is not a reason for birth at 35 weeks, and preterm induction brings neonatal risks with no proven benefit.
The trace already meets every normal criterion with a good signal, so recording for longer adds no information about her placental reserve.
A Kleihauer-Betke test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage, which would be suspected with a sinusoidal or abnormal trace, trauma or bleeding, and none of these is present here.

questions.stem:
A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after vomiting about 400 mL of bright red blood at home. He has passed black stools for 2 days. He has drunk about 10 standard drinks of beer daily for 20 years, and his last drink was last night. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse is 116/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented. He has spider naevi on his chest and palmar erythema. The abdomen has shifting dullness, and the spleen tip is palpable. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and a crystalloid bolus is started. Laboratory studies show:
Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130–180)
Platelets 74 x10^9/L (150–400)
INR 1.9 (0.9–1.2)
Urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.5)
Creatinine 90 µmol/L (60–110)
Albumin 26 g/L (35–50)
The gastroenterology registrar plans endoscopy within the next few hours.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
Pantoprazole infusion as the only drug therapy
Red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L
questions.explanation: This man has an upper GI bleed with features of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis and portal hypertension: ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, low platelets, a raised INR and a low albumin. His tachycardia and borderline blood pressure point to significant blood loss. The bleed should be treated as variceal until endoscopy shows otherwise. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) and Baveno VII, a vasoactive drug (terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours, or octreotide) should start as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected, before endoscopy. It lowers portal pressure, improves control of bleeding and reduces mortality. Patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding should also get antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily). This reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and death. Endoscopic band ligation should follow within 12 hours. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis, and the extra volume can raise portal pressure. A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does nothing for a variceal bleed and would delay vasoactive therapy and antibiotics. Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding. Balloon tamponade is wrong at this stage because it is a temporary bridge for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy.
why: Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis, eTG advises against routinely correcting it, and the extra volume raises portal pressure.
A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does not lower portal pressure or treat a variceal bleed, and it leaves out the vasoactive drug and antibiotics the guidelines require.
Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding.
Balloon tamponade is wrong because it is only a temporary rescue for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy, and endoscopy is already planned.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presents to a general practice in Perth with a 7-week history of cough productive of yellow phlegm. For the past week the phlegm has been streaked with blood. He reports drenching night sweats and has lost 6 kg without trying. He was born in the Philippines, moved to Australia 4 years ago and works as a cleaner. He has no medical history, takes no regular medicines and has never smoked. His temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There are crackles over the left upper zone, and there is no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. White cell count is 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP is 41 mg/L (<5) and HIV serology is negative. A chest X-ray shows patchy opacification with a small cavity at the left apex. He has been given a surgical mask and moved to a separate room.
questions.ask: Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay on peripheral blood
Tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, culture and NAAT
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest
questions.explanation: This man has had a productive cough for more than 3 weeks, with haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss. He was born in a country with high TB rates, and his chest X-ray shows a cavity in the upper lobe. This is active pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. The X-ray supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Confirmation needs microbiology. The Australian guidelines (CDNA SoNG, the state TB programs and eTG Antibiotic) recommend 3 sputum samples collected at least 8 hours apart, with at least 1 taken first thing in the morning. Each sample has acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT, such as Xpert MTB/RIF). Smear microscopy and NAAT give a quick answer. NAAT also tells M. tuberculosis apart from non-tuberculous mycobacteria and detects rifampicin resistance. Culture is the gold standard and gives full drug-susceptibility results. A cavity usually means a high bacterial load, so expectorated sputum is very likely to be positive. The samples should be collected outdoors or in a well-ventilated room, away from other people. He also needs urgent referral to the state TB service and notification.
why: An interferon-gamma release assay shows immune sensitisation to M. tuberculosis, but it cannot tell latent infection from active disease, and a negative result does not exclude active TB.
A tuberculin skin test cannot tell latent infection from active disease, can be falsely positive after BCG vaccination (common in people born in the Philippines), and needs a second visit.
CT shows the cavity and the extent of disease in more detail, but it provides no microbiological confirmation or susceptibility results and does not change the need for sputum testing.

Bronchoscopy with lavage is invasive and carries a risk of spreading infection to staff, so it is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose sputum samples are negative despite strong suspicion.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of burning central chest pain that began 90 minutes after a large dinner. For 6 weeks he has had similar pain on most evenings. It is worse when he lies flat and partly eased by over-the-counter antacids, and he has acid regurgitation. For the past month, bread and steak have felt as if they stick behind his sternum. His weight has fallen from 84 kg to 79 kg over 3 months without dieting. He drinks about 4 standard drinks daily, stopped smoking 10 years ago and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 98% on room air. He has mild epigastric tenderness and no palpable lymph nodes. A 12-lead ECG recorded during pain is normal. High-sensitivity troponin I is 2 ng/L at 0 hours and 2 ng/L at 2 hours (99th percentile 26 ng/L). Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 130 to 180 g/L).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Eight-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor
Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori
questions.explanation: The ECG taken during pain is normal, and high-sensitivity troponin is very low and unchanged at 0 and 2 hours, so acute MI is ruled out and this man is at low risk of acute coronary syndrome. His symptoms fit gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: burning retrosternal pain after meals that is worse lying flat, with acid regurgitation. He also has two alarm features. One is new dysphagia to solids. The other is unintentional loss of 5 kg, which is about 6% of his body weight. Daily alcohol and past smoking add to his risk. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (Gastrointestinal), alarm features call for an urgent gastroscopy rather than empirical treatment. The aim is to find or rule out the serious complications of reflux, such as peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and to take biopsies. The most important thing to prevent here is a missed or late diagnosis of cancer. A PPI can be started after the scope is booked, but it does not replace the scope.
why: An empirical PPI trial is only for reflux without alarm features, and it can ease symptoms and heal the mucosa, which delays and hides the diagnosis of cancer.
A normal ECG during pain and unchanged troponin well below the 99th percentile mean he is low risk, and his symptoms are not cardiac, so coronary imaging does not deal with the main danger.
A barium swallow can show narrowing but cannot take a biopsy, and it is not first-line for dysphagia with weight loss, so it would only delay the gastroscopy he needs.
Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for dyspepsia without alarm features, and it does not investigate dysphagia or weight loss.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward on the morning he is due to go home. Two days ago he came to the emergency department after suddenly passing a large volume of painless maroon blood with clots. He had one more small bleed in the department and none since. He has type 2 diabetes and knee osteoarthritis. He takes metformin. For the past 3 months he has also taken an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory tablet most days for knee pain. He takes no other medicines. Today his temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (his baseline is 138 g/L; reference range 130 to 180 g/L). Colonoscopy after bowel preparation showed many diverticula in the sigmoid and descending colon, with no inflammation, active bleeding, polyp or tumour. He asks how he can lower the chance of this happening again.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to reduce his risk of recurrent bleeding?
questions.explanation: This man had a self-limiting diverticular bleed. It was sudden, painless and large, with maroon blood and clots, and colonoscopy showed diverticulosis with no other source. Diverticular bleeding often recurs, in roughly 20 to 40% of patients over the following years. Non-aspirin NSAIDs are a well-established risk factor that can be changed. They raise the risk of a first diverticular bleed and of a repeat bleed. The British Society of Gastroenterology lower GI bleeding guideline advises stopping non-aspirin NSAIDs after a diverticular bleed, and Australian guidance (eTG) also advises avoiding NSAIDs in diverticular disease. The over-the-counter anti-inflammatory he takes every day should therefore be stopped, and regular paracetamol used for his osteoarthritis pain instead. Other sensible advice is a high-fibre diet with enough fluid, and returning urgently if he bleeds again. Avoiding nuts and seeds is an old myth, and large cohort studies show no added risk of bleeding or diverticulitis. Mesalazine does not prevent diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticulitis. A proton pump inhibitor protects the stomach and duodenum but has no effect on bleeding from colonic diverticular vessels. Surgery is kept for recurrent severe bleeding, or bleeding that endoscopy and embolisation cannot control. It is not used after a first bleed that stopped by itself.
why: Studies show nuts, seeds and popcorn do not raise the risk of diverticular bleeding or diverticulitis, so this restriction does not help.
Mesalazine has no proven role in preventing diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticular disease.
A proton pump inhibitor protects against upper GI bleeding from NSAIDs but does nothing for bleeding from colonic diverticula.
Elective colectomy is kept for recurrent or uncontrollable bleeding and is not offered after a first bleed that stopped by itself.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the fetal medicine clinic at 17 weeks pregnant to discuss her amniocentesis result. She conceived naturally. At 10 weeks, whole-genome cell-free DNA screening (fetal fraction 11%) showed a low chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and of sex chromosome conditions, and a high chance of trisomy 16. A 7-week scan had shown one gestational sac. The 12-week scan was normal, with a nuchal translucency of 1.4 mm. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks, with QF-PCR and chromosomal microarray, showed a normal female result with no trisomy 16. Both of her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated. She has no medical history, does not smoke, and takes folic acid and iodine. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Ultrasound today shows a single live fetus with biometry consistent with dates, no anomaly seen, normal amniotic fluid and a high posterior placenta. She is blood group O RhD positive, and her antibody screen is negative.
questions.ask: This patient is at greatest risk of which of the following complications later in this pregnancy?
questions.explanation: The screening result was valid (adequate fetal fraction) and showed a high chance of trisomy 16, but amniocentesis found a chromosomally normal fetus. The vanishing twin explanation is unlikely because she conceived naturally and an early scan showed one sac. The most likely explanation is therefore confined placental mosaicism (CPM): the trisomic cells are in the placenta, which supplies most of the cell-free DNA. RANZCOG/HGSA (C-Obs 59) and ISPD advise amniocentesis rather than CVS for rare autosomal trisomies for exactly this reason, because the placenta itself is likely to be abnormal. CPM involving chromosome 16 is strongly linked with placental dysfunction, which raises the risk of intrauterine growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and stillbirth. A normal amniocentesis result means the fetus is reassuring, but the pregnancy is still high risk. She needs continued care with a fetal medicine or obstetric team, serial growth and Doppler scans in the second half of pregnancy, blood pressure monitoring, and counselling to report reduced fetal movements. Many units also consider low-dose aspirin.
why: Her only risk factor is mild advanced maternal age, with a normal BMI and uncomplicated previous pregnancies, and placental mosaicism does not cause gestational diabetes.
After amniocentesis, leaking of fluid is uncommon and usually happens within days, so a procedure done a week ago with normal fluid today adds little later risk.
Placental dysfunction from trisomy 16 mosaicism tends to reduce amniotic fluid rather than increase it, and no fetal anomaly or diabetes is present to cause polyhydramnios.
She is RhD positive with a negative antibody screen, so the invasive procedure carries essentially no risk of clinically important sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman has been on the stroke unit for 2 days. She woke on the day of admission unable to see objects on her right. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and is otherwise well. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily was started on admission. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 86/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg and weight 68 kg. Each eye tested separately shows a congruous right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. She has no limb weakness, sensory loss or dysphasia. MRI brain shows a 30 × 20 mm acute infarct in the left medial occipital lobe with no haemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging. MR angiography shows an occluded left P2 segment and no carotid stenosis. ECG shows atrial fibrillation; an ECG 3 years ago showed sinus rhythm. Echocardiography shows no valve disease. Haemoglobin is 134 g/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L (eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73m²) and INR 1.0.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to reduce her risk of recurrent stroke?
options: Aspirin 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg orally daily
Enoxaparin bridging to warfarin, target INR 2 to 3
questions.explanation: This woman has had a cardioembolic posterior cerebral artery infarct caused by newly found non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is at least 5 (age 75 or over, hypertension, stroke), so her biggest risk is another embolic stroke. The Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management and eTG recommend oral anticoagulation, preferably with a DOAC rather than warfarin, for ischaemic stroke with AF. The stroke team times the start by infarct size, and with no haemorrhage on MRI an early start is reasonable. Apixaban is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily only if two of these apply: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. She meets none, so she needs the full dose of 5 mg twice daily. Underdosing is a common error that leaves patients unprotected. Antiplatelet therapy, alone or in combination, does much less to prevent AF-related stroke and does not replace anticoagulation. Bridging with heparin raises the risk of bleeding, including haemorrhagic change in the infarct, and gives no extra protection.
why: Wrong: she meets none of the criteria for the reduced dose, so 2.5 mg twice daily would underdose her and leave her poorly protected from another embolic stroke.
Wrong: short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA, and it prevents AF-related stroke much less well than anticoagulation while still causing bleeding.
Wrong: aspirin alone gives little protection from cardioembolic stroke in AF and is not a substitute for anticoagulation in a patient without contraindications.
Wrong: DOACs are preferred to warfarin in non-valvular AF, and heparin bridging after an acute infarct raises the risk of haemorrhagic transformation without lowering early recurrence.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of headaches for 7 weeks. They began when she started working 12-hour shifts at a desk to meet the end-of-financial-year deadline at her accounting firm. Before this she had only occasional mild headaches. The headache is a bilateral, band-like tightness that builds through the afternoon. She rates it 4/10. It now comes on every afternoon. She has no nausea or photophobia, and climbing stairs does not make it worse. She takes paracetamol 1 g about five times a week and ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a week, which takes the edge off it. She drinks four standard drinks a week and does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Her trapezius and temporalis muscles are tender. Passive neck flexion is full and painless. Fundoscopy shows sharp discs with venous pulsations, and the neurological examination is normal.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to prevent progression of her headache disorder?
options: Switch to paracetamol with codeine on headache days
Take ibuprofen 400 mg regularly three times a day
Start amitriptyline 10 mg each night as prevention
Use sumatriptan 50 mg at the onset of each attack
Limit acute pain relief to fewer than 10 days per month
questions.explanation: This woman has tension-type headache: it is bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate and not made worse by activity, she has no nausea or photophobia, her pericranial muscles are tender, and it started with a clear trigger (long hours at a desk under deadline stress). Her examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. The main risk for her is medication-overuse headache. She is already taking simple analgesics on about 25 to 35 days in every 4 weeks. ICHD-3 defines medication-overuse headache as headache on 15 or more days a month with regular overuse for more than 3 months. The threshold is 15 or more days a month for simple analgesics, and 10 or more days a month for triptans, opioids or combination analgesics. At 7 weeks she has not met the time criterion yet, but she is well over the frequency threshold. Following eTG, she should keep acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month (roughly 2 to 3 days a week), keep a headache diary, and avoid codeine. Treatment should be mainly non-drug: posture and ergonomics, regular breaks, sleep, exercise, physiotherapy and stress management.
why: Codeine-containing combination products cause medication-overuse headache at a lower threshold (10 or more days a month), cause dependence, and eTG advises avoiding opioids in tension-type headache.
Taking ibuprofen regularly every day guarantees analgesic overuse, which raises her risk of medication-overuse headache as well as gastrointestinal and kidney harm.
Preventive amitriptyline is kept for established chronic tension-type headache that has not responded to non-drug measures, and it does nothing about her current analgesic overuse.
Triptans do not work for tension-type headache and cause medication-overuse headache at only 10 or more days a month, so taking one with every daily attack would make things worse.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a 1-day history of worsening headache, fever, vomiting and photophobia. For 5 days before this he had right ear pain. He has no medical history, takes no medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, respirations 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. He has neck stiffness, no rash, sharp optic discs and no focal neurological deficit. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging. Blood cultures are taken and a lumbar puncture is done. Ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg are given straight after the procedure. Results:
Blood: leucocytes 19.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 185 mg/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L
CSF: turbid; opening pressure 28 cmH2O; white cells 1900 x10^6/L (90% polymorphs); red cells 6 x10^6/L; protein 2.1 g/L (0.15 to 0.45); glucose 1.2 mmol/L; Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
questions.explanation: The CSF is turbid, with many polymorphs, a high protein and a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 1.2/6.0 = 0.2 (below 0.4), so this is bacterial meningitis. Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the probable source is his right acute otitis media. Some pneumococci have reduced susceptibility to penicillin and ceftriaxone. So eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone as soon as Gram-positive diplococci are seen, and continuing both until susceptibility results are back. Treatment is then narrowed to suit the organism. Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days, because it gives the most benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. Amoxicillin covers Listeria and is added only for patients at risk: those over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or with alcohol dependence. He has none of these risks, and Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus, not a diplococcus. Aciclovir is not needed: he has no confusion, seizures or focal signs, and the CSF picture is clearly bacterial with organisms seen. Changing to benzylpenicillin before susceptibility is known risks undertreating a resistant strain.
why: Amoxicillin covers Listeria, which shows as Gram-positive bacilli and is a risk only in people over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or alcohol-dependent, and he is none of these.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis, but he has no encephalitic features and the CSF is clearly bacterial, with organisms seen.
Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days in pneumococcal meningitis because this is the organism where it most reduces death and hearing loss.
Narrowing to benzylpenicillin is done only after susceptibility testing confirms a sensitive strain, so changing now could undertreat a resistant pneumococcus.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a rural hospital 3 hours after central chest pressure began. The pain spreads to his left arm, and he has sweating and nausea. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He drinks about 4 standard drinks per week and has had no falls, injections or strenuous exercise. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 150/92 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Jugular venous pressure is not raised, the chest is clear, and there is no hepatomegaly or peripheral oedema. An ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V4. A chest X-ray shows clear lungs. Blood taken from a newly inserted cannula shows: potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2); bilirubin 10 µmol/L (<20); ALT 28 U/L (<45); AST 71 U/L (<35); ALP 80 U/L (30–110); GGT 30 U/L (<50); creatine kinase 590 U/L (<200); hs-troponin T 210 ng/L (<14).
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's aspartate aminotransferase (AST) result?
options: In vitro haemolysis of the blood sample
questions.explanation: The AST is raised on its own. ALT, bilirubin, ALP and GGT are all normal, and this happens alongside an anterior STEMI, a raised creatine kinase and an hs-troponin T well above the 99th percentile. AST is found in cardiac muscle as well as in liver and skeletal muscle. It leaks from infarcting myocardium, which is why it was once used as a cardiac marker. ALT is much more specific to the liver, so a normal ALT with a normal cholestatic profile points away from liver disease. Here the AST is best read as part of the myocardial infarction. It does not need liver work-up, and it must not delay reperfusion. Troponin, not AST, is the marker to follow for myocardial injury.
why: Wrong: an AST:ALT ratio above 2 can suggest alcohol, but he drinks very little, and his GGT and ALT are normal.
Wrong: congestive hepatopathy needs raised right-sided pressures, but his JVP is normal, there is no hepatomegaly or oedema, his lungs are clear, and ALT and bilirubin would usually rise too.
Wrong: in vitro haemolysis would also raise the potassium, which is normal at 4.1 mmol/L, and the sample came from a fresh cannula.
Wrong: he has had no trauma, falls, injections or exertion, and the raised troponin with ST elevation places the enzyme source in the heart, not skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 50 minutes of heavy central chest pain that began while she was watching television. Over the past fortnight her known angina has come on with less exertion, and she now needs glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) most days. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin and aspirin. In the ED she has received aspirin 300 mg, three sublingual GTN doses and intravenous morphine, and an intravenous GTN infusion has been titrated for the past 20 minutes. She still rates the pain 7/10 and is diaphoretic. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg in both arms, respirations 18/min and SpO2 96% on room air. Two 12-lead ECGs taken 15 minutes apart show sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. High-sensitivity troponin I, taken 40 minutes after onset, is 9 ng/L (99th percentile for women 16 ng/L). Chest X-ray is normal.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: This woman has a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. She has crescendo angina and prolonged rest pain. Her pain is still going after aspirin, repeated sublingual GTN, opioid and a titrated IV GTN infusion. The 2016 National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guideline, which eTG follows, classes ongoing or recurrent ischaemic pain that does not respond to medical treatment as very high risk. This applies whatever the ECG or troponin shows. Very high-risk patients need invasive coronary angiography, with revascularisation if indicated, within 2 hours. Arrange this urgently with cardiology, including the choice of P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulant. A normal ECG and a normal troponin taken 40 minutes after onset do not lower her risk, because both can be normal early in a myocardial infarction. Repeat troponin, CT coronary angiography and stress testing are for patients whose pain has settled and who are at low or intermediate risk. Fibrinolysis is only for STEMI.
why: Serial troponin helps decide between unstable angina and NSTEMI, but the result would not change her management, because refractory pain already makes her very high risk.
Fibrinolysis gives no benefit and may cause harm in non-ST-elevation ACS, and her ECGs show no ST elevation.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 5 months of worsening breathlessness. Over this time he has lost 20 kg, has coughed up blood-tinged sputum and his voice has become hoarse. He has COPD, and his triple-therapy inhaler has not helped. He has smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 50 years and worked for decades as a mechanic. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 29/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg and SpO2 is 92% on room air. He has finger clubbing and a hard right supraclavicular lymph node. On the right side of the chest, expansion is reduced, percussion is stony dull and breath sounds are absent. The trachea is deviated to the left. An erect PA chest X-ray, not rotated, shows a large right effusion with a meniscus reaching the 2nd anterior rib, which obscures the right heart border and hilum. The trachea and mediastinum are displaced to the left. The left lung is clear.
questions.ask: Which of the following best explains the position of the trachea and mediastinum on this film?
options: Paratracheal nodal mass displacing the airway
questions.explanation: The film shows a large right effusion with the trachea and mediastinum pushed to the left, away from the fluid. Being pushed away from the fluid means the effusion has a mass effect: the fluid takes up enough space in the right hemithorax to move the mediastinum across. For this patient, it means the shift is not explained by a major right-sided collapse, so a central obstructing tumour has not pulled the mediastinum back towards the right. It also means the mediastinum is not held in place by pleural tumour. So ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration (no more than about 1.5 L at a time) is likely to ease his breathlessness, and it also gives fluid for diagnosis. A contrast CT chest should ideally be done before the effusion is fully drained. If a very large effusion had no shift, or the mediastinum had moved towards the effusion, that would suggest lobar or lung collapse from an endobronchial tumour, or a mediastinum fixed by mesothelioma or malignant nodes. In that case drainage would help less and could cause problems, and bronchoscopy should be considered. Tension pneumothorax is ruled out because the film shows a meniscus, not air.
why: Collapse causes volume loss, which pulls the trachea and mediastinum towards the affected (right) side, not away from it.
A mediastinum encased by pleural tumour, as in mesothelioma, cannot move, so a large effusion would cause little or no shift.
Hyperinflation in COPD affects both lungs and does not push the mediastinum sideways, and the left lung is described as clear.
A paratracheal nodal mass widens the mediastinum and may narrow the trachea, but it would not shift the whole mediastinum away from a large right effusion.

A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner to discuss blood test results. She has had four months of tiredness, cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain of 5 kg. She has had type 1 diabetes since age 11 and uses insulin glargine and insulin aspart. She drinks about 4 standard drinks a week and rarely eats fresh vegetables. Her pulse is 58/min and blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg. She has a diffuse, firm, non-tender goitre and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes. Vibration sense, joint position sense and gait are normal. Investigations show:
Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115–165)
MCV 116 fL (80–100)
TSH 38 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
Free T4 5.1 pmol/L (10–20)
Anti-TPO antibodies strongly positive
Morning cortisol 430 nmol/L (normal)
Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L
Serum folate 4.0 nmol/L (above 7)
Serum vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor antibodies: pending

options: Adrenal crisis from unmasked cortisol deficiency
Secondary iron overload from rapid erythropoiesis
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

An MCV of 116 fL is too high to blame on hypothyroidism alone, and her B12 result is still pending. So the anaemia looks better while B12-related demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration) gets worse, and that damage can be permanent. Australian guidance (eTG) says folate must not be given alone until B12 deficiency has been ruled out or is being treated. A low folate with a normal neurological examination does not remove this risk, because she could be low in both. Safe options are to wait for the B12 result or to give B12 alongside folate.

Adrenal crisis is the risk when levothyroxine, not folic acid, is started in untreated Addison disease, and her normal morning cortisol and electrolytes make adrenal insufficiency unlikely.
Correcting megaloblastic anaemia uses up iron and can cause iron deficiency, not iron overload.
Gastric cancer is a long-term risk of pernicious anaemia itself, and starting folic acid neither causes it nor speeds it up.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because her breathlessness has been getting worse for 6 weeks. She now gets breathless walking to her letterbox. She sleeps on three pillows and wakes at night gasping for air. She has had no chest pain, sweating or palpitations. She had a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction 5 months ago and has had hypertension for 30 years. Her medicines are aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril and metoprolol. Her pulse is 100/min and regular, blood pressure is 158/90 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 22/min and SpO2 is 94% on room air. Her jugular venous pressure is raised, her apex beat is displaced and there are crackles at both lung bases. Serum potassium is 4.3 mmol/L (reference 3.5 to 5.2). A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm at 100/min and a QRS duration of 94 ms. The S wave in V1 plus the R wave in V5 measures 41 mm. There is downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. These changes are the same as on her ECG at hospital discharge 5 months ago.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the ST-segment and T-wave changes on this ECG?
options: Subendocardial ischaemia from a new acute coronary syndrome
Delayed ventricular depolarisation from left bundle branch block
Abnormal repolarisation caused by a low serum potassium
Left ventricular hypertrophy with secondary repolarisation changes
Characteristic ST-segment scooping caused by digoxin therapy
questions.explanation: The S wave in V1 plus the R wave in V5 adds up to 41 mm, which is more than the Sokolow-Lyon threshold of 35 mm. This meets the voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). With LVH, downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T-wave inversion in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) is the classic secondary repolarisation ('strain') pattern. It fits her 30 years of hypertension and her displaced apex. The changes are the same as on her discharge ECG 5 months ago, so they are long-standing and not acute. Her new decompensated heart failure still needs hospital assessment, including a troponin and an echocardiogram. The ECG itself, though, shows chronic changes from LVH, not new ischaemia. New ischaemia is unlikely because there is no chest pain and the ST-T changes are the same as 5 months ago, although a troponin is still needed. Left bundle branch block is excluded because the QRS is 94 ms, and the diagnosis needs a QRS of 120 ms or more. Hypokalaemia is excluded because her potassium is normal at 4.3 mmol/L; it also typically causes U waves and flattened T waves. Digoxin is not one of her medicines, and its effect is a scooped (reverse-tick) ST segment, not the asymmetric T-wave inversion seen with LVH voltages.
why: There is no chest pain and the ST-T changes are the same as on the discharge ECG, so they do not point to new ischaemia, although a troponin is still needed.
A QRS duration of 94 ms rules out left bundle branch block, which needs a QRS of at least 120 ms.
Her serum potassium is normal at 4.3 mmol/L, and hypokalaemia typically causes U waves and flattened T waves, not this pattern.
She does not take digoxin, and digoxin causes a scooped ST segment, not asymmetric lateral T-wave inversion with high QRS voltages.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, and 1 day of vomiting. He has no past medical history. He weighs 36 kg. His first venous blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34.0 mmol/L and sodium 131 mmol/L. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.8 mmol/L and urea is 13.2 mmol/L. Fluid replacement is started, and 1 hour later an insulin infusion is started at 0.1 units/kg/h. Five hours after arrival he says he has a severe headache, vomits, and becomes irritable and confused. His pulse is 58/min (130/min on arrival), blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min, SpO2 is 98% on room air and temperature is 36.9 °C. GCS is 11 (E3 V3 M5). His pupils are equal and reactive. Repeat glucose is 15.2 mmol/L and sodium is 129 mmol/L. The head of the bed is raised and the fluid rate is reduced.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain now
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV over 1 hour
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Cease the insulin infusion until review
questions.explanation: This boy has severe DKA as his first presentation of type 1 diabetes. He has the main risk factors for cerebral oedema: young age, new diagnosis, pH below 7.1, a high urea, and a sodium that is falling instead of rising as the glucose comes down. Several hours into treatment he has a headache, vomiting, a falling GCS and a new low heart rate with high blood pressure (Cushing response). This is a clinical diagnosis of cerebral oedema. The RCH DKA guideline says to treat it straight away, without waiting for imaging. Raise the head of the bed, reduce the fluid rate, and give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 20%) IV over 20 minutes. Hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg is an alternative. Call ICU early for airway support, and do a CT only after he is stable, to look for other causes such as a clot or bleed. CT now is wrong because imaging delays treatment that can save his life, and cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically. Sodium bicarbonate is wrong because it does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself linked to cerebral oedema. Dexamethasone is wrong because steroids do not help this kind of brain swelling and they make hyperglycaemia worse. Stopping the insulin is wrong because the ketosis needs ongoing insulin to clear; the rate may be lowered, but the infusion should not be stopped to treat cerebral oedema.
why: Wrong: CT delays urgent treatment for a diagnosis made clinically; image only once he is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema.
Wrong: corticosteroids have no role in cerebral oedema from DKA and would worsen his hyperglycaemia.
Wrong: insulin is still needed to clear the ketosis, and stopping it does not treat the raised intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after a sudden, severe occipital headache that began while he was jogging. Two weeks ago he had a severe headache that settled within 30 minutes. He has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension, treated with perindopril. On arrival, his temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 82/min, respirations 16/min, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13 (E3 V4 M6). He has neck stiffness and bilateral subhyaloid haemorrhages on fundoscopy, and no focal deficit. INR is 1.0 and platelets are 245 x10^9/L. Non-contrast CT shows diffuse blood in the basal cisterns, spreading into the ventricles, with dilated temporal horns. CT angiography shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Forty-five minutes later he vomits. His GCS is now 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 48/min, blood pressure 204/96 mm Hg and respirations 12/min and irregular. His pupils are still equal and reactive.
questions.ask: Which of the following best explains the change in his vital signs?
questions.explanation: This man has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood has spread into his ventricles, and the dilated temporal horns show early hydrocephalus. Since arrival his GCS has fallen. He now has a rising systolic pressure, a slow heart rate and irregular breathing. This is Cushing's triad, a late sign that intracranial pressure is raised and the brainstem is being compressed, which means coning is imminent. Equal pupils do not rule this out, because pupil changes can come late. Do not read the rising blood pressure as something to treat on its own. It is the brain's attempt to keep up cerebral perfusion pressure, and lowering it hard could make ischaemia worse. Under eTG guidance and the Between the Flags criteria, this needs an immediate rapid response call, airway assessment, the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees, and an urgent neurosurgical review for an external ventricular drain. Delayed cerebral ischaemia usually happens on days 3 to 14, not within hours of the bleed. A hypertensive emergency does not explain the slow heart rate or the fall in GCS, and on arrival his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg. A vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure. Neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge typically causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and heart failure.
why: Wrong: delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not 3 hours after the headache began.
Wrong: a hypertensive emergency would not cause a falling heart rate or irregular breathing, and his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg before his GCS fell.
Wrong: a vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure, and it would not cause a lasting fall in GCS or irregular breathing.
Wrong: neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge usually causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and pulmonary oedema, not a slow heart rate with severe hypertension.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father with 4 days of forceful vomiting after every feed. The vomit is milky and has never been green. He feeds eagerly straight after vomiting and has had 2 wet nappies in the past 24 hours. He was born at term and is formula fed. He weighs 4.5 kg, down from 4.9 kg 2 weeks ago. His hands and feet are cool and capillary refill time is 3 seconds. A peripheral cannula is placed. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 18 mm.
questions.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

0.9% sodium chloride 45 mL intravenously over 15 minutes
Potassium chloride 2.25 mmol intravenously over 1 hour
Hydrocortisone 25 mg intravenously as a single dose
Laparoscopic pyloromyotomy on the next available list
questions.explanation: This boy has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The ultrasound shows a muscle wall of 5 mm or more (abnormal is 3 mm or more) and a channel of 18 mm (abnormal is 15 mm or more), and he has the typical hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. He is also in compensated shock: he is tachycardic, drowsy and cool at the hands and feet, with a capillary refill time of 3 seconds, while his blood pressure is still normal. Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency but a surgical urgency, not a surgical emergency. The first step is to treat the shock. Keep him nil by mouth and give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (45 mL for 4.5 kg), then reassess. After that, give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, and add potassium once he is passing urine (RCH Pyloric stenosis, Dehydration and Intravenous fluids guidelines). Surgery waits until the bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal, because operating while he is still alkalotic risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

Wrong: potassium is replaced only after perfusion is restored and he is passing urine, and it does not treat the shock.
Wrong: his low potassium and alkalosis are the opposite of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which causes a high potassium and an acidosis, so steroids are not needed.
Wrong: pyloromyotomy should wait until shock and the alkalosis are corrected, because operating sooner risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

questions.stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to a general practice in regional Victoria with a 6-week history of cough. The cough is wet and happens by day and by night. It has not improved with 7 days of amoxicillin or with inhaled salbutamol through a spacer. His mother remembers that the cough started on the evening of a family barbecue. While eating popcorn there, he coughed and gagged for a short time and then settled. He has no eczema and no previous wheeze. He is fully immunised and has had no contact with tuberculosis. He is playful. His temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 120/min, respirations 38/min, and SpO2 96% in room air. On examination there is reduced air entry and a fixed monophonic wheeze over the left lower zone only. A chest X-ray shows a hyperinflated left lung with the mediastinum shifted to the right. No radio-opaque object is seen.
questions.ask: If the underlying cause is not treated, this child is most at risk of which of the following complications?
questions.explanation: This toddler has an inhaled foreign body, most likely a popcorn kernel, in the left lower lobe bronchus. The clues are a choking episode at the start, a cough that has lasted weeks despite antibiotics and bronchodilators, one-sided monophonic wheeze with reduced air entry, and air trapping on the same side with the mediastinum pushed away. Organic objects are radiolucent, so a normal-looking X-ray does not rule out the diagnosis. Organic material left in the bronchus causes ongoing local inflammation, granulation tissue and infection beyond the blockage. This leads to recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe and then permanent damage to the airway: bronchiectasis. The risk goes up the longer the object stays in. This is why the RCH guideline recommends prompt rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia at a paediatric centre, rather than more courses of antibiotics or inhalers. Tension pneumothorax is a rare acute event, not the expected result of an object left in place. Tracheo-oesophageal fistula is a complication of an oesophageal foreign body, especially a button battery, not a bronchial one. Pulmonary arterial hypertension needs widespread lung or vascular disease, not one blocked lobe. Asthma is not caused by a foreign body, and the poor response to salbutamol argues against it.
why: Wrong: air trapping can rarely rupture into the pleura, but this is an uncommon acute event and not the usual consequence of a retained object.
Wrong: a fistula forms when an oesophageal foreign body such as a button battery erodes into the trachea, not from an object in the bronchus.
Wrong: pulmonary arterial hypertension needs widespread lung or vascular disease, and one blocked lobe does not cause it.
Wrong: a foreign body does not cause atopic asthma, and this child has no atopy, no earlier wheeze and no response to salbutamol.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of yellow eyes and dark urine. Two weeks ago he developed fever, anorexia and aching wrists and knees, which have since eased. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 3 months ago. He takes no medicines and drinks 6 standard drinks a week. Temperature is 37.6 °C, BP 124/78 mmHg, pulse 88/min and respiratory rate 14/min. He is alert, with scleral icterus, a tender smooth liver edge and no asterixis, and he is tolerating oral fluids. Bilirubin is 142 µmol/L (<20), ALT 2140 U/L (<40), ALP 165 U/L (30–110) and INR 1.1 (0.9–1.2). Paracetamol is undetectable. Ultrasound shows a 4 mm common bile duct without stones. HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive, anti-HBs is negative, and hepatitis A IgM and HCV antibody are negative.

options: Supportive care and repeat hepatic testing in clinic
questions.explanation: This man has acute hepatitis B. He had a likely sexual exposure within the 1 to 6 month incubation period, then a prodrome with arthralgia, then jaundice. His tests show a hepatocellular pattern, and HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive. His liver is still working well: INR is 1.1, he is alert with no asterixis, and he is drinking. So he has no features of severe hepatitis or acute liver failure. More than 95% of immunocompetent adults with acute hepatitis B clear the virus on their own. Therapeutic Guidelines and ASHM recommend supportive care for these patients. That means avoiding alcohol and liver-toxic drugs, and repeating LFTs and INR regularly until they improve, with safety-netting advice to return if he becomes confused, starts bleeding or vomits persistently. The doctor must also notify the case, arrange contact tracing (testing, vaccination, and HBIG for non-immune contacts), and repeat HBsAg at 6 months to check for chronic infection. Antivirals are only for severe acute hepatitis B: INR above 1.5, encephalopathy, or jaundice lasting more than about 4 weeks.

Tenofovir (or entecavir) is reserved for severe or protracted acute hepatitis B, such as INR above 1.5 or encephalopathy, and he has neither.
Interferon is contraindicated in acute hepatitis B because the immune flare it causes can tip an inflamed liver into decompensation, and it has no role in this self-limiting illness.
Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity or early acute liver failure, but his paracetamol level is undetectable and his INR and mental state are normal.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man collapses in the emergency department waiting area 20 minutes after triage. He had come in with 4 hours of central chest heaviness and nausea. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. His first rhythm is ventricular fibrillation. He receives CPR, three shocks, adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV. Spontaneous circulation returns after 12 minutes. He is being ventilated with a bag-valve-mask on 15 L/min oxygen. Pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, temperature is 35.6 °C and SpO2 is 97%. GCS is 3. A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V5. A venous blood gas taken 5 minutes after return of circulation shows: pH 7.09 (7.32 to 7.42); pCO2 62 mm Hg (41 to 51); bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22 to 28); base excess -11 mmol/L (-2 to +2); lactate 9.2 mmol/L (below 2.0); potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2); glucose 15.1 mmol/L (4.0 to 7.8).
questions.ask: Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base disturbance?

Acute respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with coexisting metabolic alkalosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
questions.explanation: The pH of 7.09 shows a severe acidaemia. There are two causes, and each one lowers the pH. First, the pCO2 of 62 mm Hg is high even for a venous sample, so there is a respiratory acidosis. This comes from low cardiac output during the arrest and poor ventilation with the bag-valve-mask. Second, the bicarbonate of 18 mmol/L, base excess of -11 and lactate of 9.2 mmol/L show a lactic metabolic acidosis from 12 minutes of low tissue perfusion. If the lungs were compensating for the metabolic acidosis, Winter's formula (1.5 x 18 + 8 = 35 +/- 2 mm Hg) says the pCO2 should be low. Instead it is high, so a second, respiratory process is present. This matters for his care. ANZCOR post-resuscitation guidance asks for normocapnia, so his ventilation should be increased and adjusted to arterial gases. Do not give bicarbonate routinely. The lactate should clear once perfusion improves with reperfusion and blood pressure support (MAP at least 65 mm Hg). The mild rise in potassium and the high glucose are expected after an arrest.
why: Wrong: if the lungs were compensating, the pCO2 would be about 35 mm Hg, but it is 62 mm Hg, so there is also a respiratory acidosis.
Wrong: renal compensation would raise the bicarbonate, and the kidneys need days to do this, but his bicarbonate is low at 18 mmol/L.
Wrong: he has nothing that causes a metabolic alkalosis, such as vomiting or diuretics, and his low bicarbonate and base excess show only a metabolic acidosis.
Wrong: in chronic respiratory acidosis the bicarbonate is raised and the pH is close to normal, but he has a low bicarbonate and severe acidaemia after an acute event.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in general practice. Eight years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% from metformin non-adherence, gradual symmetrical stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg and loss of protective sensation.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man in the emergency department. questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

why: Heart sounds are not muffled, the trachea is deviated, and the left chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds on one side; a normal cardiac silhouette does not exclude acute tamponade, so eFAST is still needed.
